systemPrompt:
You are an assistant helping a developer with their CircleCI projects. Answer the user's question using only the tools provided to you. Ground every claim in data you actually retrieved; if you cannot retrieve something, say so. Do not change anything in the project beyond what the user explicitly asks for. Finish with a clear, direct answer to the question.

The current directory is a checkout of the CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli repository. You can inspect its files with the read-only list_files and read_file tools.

This server exposes CircleCI: the CI pipelines an org runs, the deploys those
pipelines produce, and the config, orbs, functions and usage data around them. Every tool
acts as the authenticated user and sees only what that user can see.

Ids are UUIDs and are not interchangeable — a run id, a workflow id and a job
id are distinct, and a tool handed the wrong kind fails rather than guessing.
Nothing accepts a job number or a CircleCI web URL. Projects and orgs are the
exception: they take either a slug ("gh/org/repo", "gh/org") or a UUID.

SKILLS. This server ships written playbooks for the work that takes several
of the tools below — the orderings, the costs and the usual mistakes, which
no single tool description can carry:

    list_skills  the catalog: what each playbook covers, and its references
    get_skill    one playbook, or one of its bundled references

Before working through the tools below, call list_skills once and load any
skill whose description covers the work, together with the related skills it
names. It takes no arguments and returns the whole catalog, so that one call
is the entire search. If nothing clearly fits, load nothing and work from the
tool descriptions. One pass serves a whole session: having listed once, do not
list again. The one exception is a failed run you hold the id of: call
get_run_failure_report first, and look for a skill only if it leaves the
cause open.

A skill earns its call at the start of a piece of work, not after one has gone
wrong. The same guides are readable as resources under circleci://skills/ for
clients that browse resources rather than call tools.

PIPELINES. The tools form a chain, each level's id feeding the next:

    list_runs -> get_run -> list_run_workflows -> get_workflow -> list_workflow_jobs -> get_job

Enter at list_runs; it is the only one of these that takes a project rather
than a UUID. With no project named, mine=true lists the user's own runs across
every project. Skip levels whenever you already hold an id — get_run is
pointless if you have the run id and want its workflows. trigger_run starts a
new run and returns its id, which enters the chain at get_run.

If you hold a run id and want to know why it failed, call
get_run_failure_report first; you do not need list_skills or any tool in the
chain before it. It walks the chain in one call and returns the failed steps
with their exit codes and condensed output, plus the job id, execution and step
num the tools below take; on a very wide run it says what it left out. Reach
for those tools only for what the report leaves open.

For the files a run stored — a coverage report, test results, a build
output — call list_run_artifacts with the run id rather than walking the chain
and calling list_job_artifacts once per job: it reads every job's artifacts in
one call, and path narrows them to the ones wanted. For the latest successful
run, take the id from list_runs with status "success" and limit 1.

DIAGNOSING A JOB. Five tools take a job id and answer different questions.
Which you pick matters more than the order:

    get_job                 which step failed and its exit code, or why it never ran
    list_job_tests          which tests failed
    get_job_logs            what a step printed
    get_job_resource_usage  whether it ran out of CPU or memory
    list_job_artifacts      the files it persisted, with download URLs

Start with get_job — it is cheap and names the failed step — unless
get_run_failure_report already did. If that step ran
tests, go to list_job_tests, which is far cheaper than logs and already
filtered to failures. Reach for get_job_logs only when you need the output
itself; it is the most expensive tool here, so keep tail_lines small. If a job
died with nothing in its logs, check get_job_resource_usage for an OOM.

FLAKY TESTS. list_flaky_tests takes a project, not a job, and answers "which
tests are flaky?" in one call: tests that failed and then passed within the
same pipeline, counted across the project's runs, most-flaked first. Reach for
it instead of walking runs and jobs to compare outcomes, and to check whether
a test that just failed is a known flake before treating it as a regression.

DEPLOYS are a separate subsystem, keyed on projects and orgs rather than on
pipeline ids, and reachable without touching a run:

    list_deployments                what was deployed — to a project, or across an org
    list_deploy_components          a project's deployable units
    list_deploy_environments        an org's release targets (production, staging)
    list_deploy_component_versions  a component's version history
    get_deploy_component            one component by id
    get_deploy_environment          one environment by id

For "what is live" or "when did X ship", use list_deployments — pass project for
a single project or org for everything in the org. The two get_ tools resolve an
id you already hold back to its name; the list tools already return names, so reach
for them only when an id arrived from somewhere else.

CONFIG, ORBS AND FUNCTIONS need no CircleCI resource at all; they work on YAML
you hold:

    validate_config  compile a config and report its errors
    get_orb          an orb's published versions — whether a pin is stale
    get_orb_source   an orb's YAML — how to call its jobs and commands
    list_functions   every published function, with its versions
    get_function     one function's arguments, versions, and the config that uses it

Read an orb's source before writing config against it, and compile a config
before pushing it rather than after. To add a function, take the declaration
and step get_function returns and edit the config yourself: nothing here
writes to it.

When writing a new config, or adding a setup or test step to one, call
list_functions first and use the matching function; write a run: step
only when none fits. Orbs remain supported for existing pipelines, so do
not move a working orb-based config to functions unless the user asks.

WRITES. trigger_run is additive: it starts a new run of a project's branch or tag.
rerun_workflow is additive: it creates a new workflow. cancel_workflow
stops running work. rollback_deploy_component redeploys production software.
Confirm with the user before calling any of them unless they asked for it
directly — and for a rollback, confirm the component, the environment and both
versions rather than just the intent.

Also: get_me for the authenticated user's identity and ids, and
download_usage_data for an org's billing CSVs (asynchronous — start an export,
then poll it).

FEEDBACK. send_feedback reports a problem with this server to CircleCI — an
error that looks like CircleCI's fault, a capability that is missing, or a
tool that misled you. Errors that look like CircleCI's fault end by pointing
to it. Report once per distinct problem, saying what you were trying to do and
what happened. It changes nothing in CircleCI, so unlike the writes above it
needs no confirmation. Report functions too: when you write a run: step
because no function does the job, or because one falls short, send it with
type and function.

When a tool errors, read the message before retrying. Most errors here say
what was wrong — the wrong kind of id, a missing project, an execution index
out of range — and the same arguments will fail the same way.

Target CircleCI project: gh/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli (organization: gh/CircleCI-Public).

## Available skills

Skills are packaged instructions for specific kinds of tasks. The following skills are available:

- circleci-builds: Diagnose and fix failing CircleCI builds quickly and safely. Use when users ask to investigate failed CircleCI jobs, triage flaky pipelines, identify root causes from logs, and implement minimal fixes in configuration, test setup, or build-related code paths.
- circleci-cli: Day-to-day CircleCI from the terminal with the circleci CLI — authenticate, validate config before you commit, watch the run your push triggered, review pipeline/workflow/job status, print a failure report for your latest failed run in one command, read job logs and failed tests, list a project's flaky tests, list or download every artifact in a run in one command, and rerun/cancel/trigger. Use when a developer asks to authenticate CLI access, check their build or pipeline status, watch a run after pushing, see why CI failed, read job output/logs, find failing tests, list flaky tests, download build outputs such as a coverage report, rerun failed jobs, cancel or re-trigger a run, validate a config change locally, or look up a project's environment variables, contexts, triggers or pipeline definitions. For first-time project connection / pipeline-definition setup use the onboarding skill; for the diagnose-and-fix methodology on a failing build use circleci-builds.
- circleci-config: Optimize CircleCI configuration for speed, reliability, and maintainability. Use when users ask to improve `.circleci/config.yml`, reduce CI runtime, tune caching/workspaces/parallelism, remove pipeline waste, or fix flaky pipeline behavior caused by configuration choices.
- circleci-deploy-setup: Set up, audit, or regenerate CircleCI deploy markers, deploy and rollback pipelines, and release validation in a repository. Use when a user wants to onboard a project to deploys, releases, deploy markers, smart deployments, release validation or auto-rollback; when they ask what deploy setup a repo already has or whether it is complete; when they want to regenerate or upgrade an existing deploy.yml, rollback.yml, or marker setup; or when they ask to replicate the Deploys setup wizard locally. Covers config generation, verification, pipeline registration, and wiring validation webhooks from Datadog, Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager, or any tool that can POST to a URL. For first-time project connection and basic pipeline setup use the onboarding skill.
- circleci-smarter-testing-debugging: Debug CircleCI Smarter Testing on a project that is already onboarded, using `circleci testsuite impact` to explore impact data (which files impact a test, which tests a file impacts) and `circleci testsuite result` to show how a job's test atoms were selected and how they ran. Use when asking why a test was selected or skipped, why a change didn't run the expected tests, why too many tests run, or how a test atom ran in a job. For first-time setup use circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding.
- circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding: Onboard a project onto CircleCI Smarter Testing — check the default suite for the detected test runner (or write `.circleci/test-suites.yml` when it doesn't fit), replace the raw test step (or legacy `circleci tests glob`/`split`/`run`) with `circleci testsuite run`, validate with `circleci testsuite doctor`, make sure the free features work (static test splitting, rerun only failed tests, test uploads), then ask if any credit-charged features should be enabled (test impact analysis, dynamic test splitting, dynamic parallelism, auto rerun failed tests). Use for first-time setup of Smarter Testing, testsuite, test-suites YAML, or migrating a test step. Not for running (circleci-smarter-testing-run) or debugging a suite that is already onboarded.
- circleci-smarter-testing-run: Run a project's tests locally through CircleCI Smarter Testing with `circleci testsuite run`, which detects the test runner when there is no `.circleci/test-suites.yml`, narrowed to a subset with `--test-atom-pattern`, instead of calling the test runner directly. Use whenever you are about to run tests (`go test`, `npm test`, `pytest`, `jest`, `vitest`, `rspec`, `gradle test` and so on) in a repository that has `.circleci/test-suites.yml` or `.circleci/config.yml`, including running one package, file or directory of tests while iterating. For first-time setup use circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding; for why a test was selected or skipped use circleci-smarter-testing-debugging.
- debug-ci-failures: Debug CircleCI build failures, analyze test results, and identify flaky tests. Use when the user says "debug CI", "why is CI failing", "fix CI failures", "find flaky tests", "what broke in CI", "check CircleCI", or asks about failing pipelines or build errors.
- onboarding: Agent-driven onboarding guide for CircleCI. Walks a user through the full setup journey: account creation, organization selection or creation, GitHub App connection, project creation, pipeline definition + trigger, and iterating a config file until it passes. Everything is done from the terminal with the circleci CLI — never send the user to the web app for something a command can do. Use this skill whenever a user says "onboard to CircleCI", "set up CircleCI", "get started with CircleCI", "connect my repo to CircleCI", "create a CircleCI project", or asks for help with any early CircleCI setup step. Also trigger if the user has a new repo and wants CI running on it. For day-to-day work on an already-connected project (watch a run, read failing logs, rerun) use the circleci-cli skill instead.

Before starting a task that matches a skill's description, call `load_skill` with the skill name to read its full instructions, then follow them using the tools available to you. If a skill references bundled files, read them with `read_skill_file`. Only load skills that are relevant to the task.

version: 2.1

functions:
  setup-go: github.com/circleci-functions/setup-go@v0.6.0

commands:
  setup:
    steps:
      - checkout
      - install-go
      - install-task

  # Installs the toolchain and restores the module, build and lint caches, saved at job end.
  install-go:
    steps:
      - setup-go:
          with:
            version-file: go.mod
            golangci-lint-cache: true
            checksum: '{{ checksum "go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "clikit/go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "tools/go.sum" }}'
      - run: go version

  install-task:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Install go-task
          command: |
            sh -c "$(curl --location https://taskfile.dev/install.sh)" -- -d -b "$HOME/.local/bin"
            echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"

  # GoReleaser's dockers_v2 pipe shells out to `docker buildx build`, so the
  # builder and the registry login have to exist before it runs.
  setup-docker:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Register QEMU for cross-architecture builds
          # Dockerfile.alpine RUNs `apk add`, once per platform in the manifest,
          # so building its arm64 half on an amd64 host needs binfmt handlers
          # registered. Idempotent, and a no-op for the cimg/base image, which
          # only COPYs.
          command: docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64
      - run:
          name: Create a buildx builder
          # The machine image's default buildx driver is `docker`, which can
          # neither build for two platforms in one invocation nor push a
          # manifest list. A docker-container driver can do both.
          command: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container
      - run:
          name: Log in to Docker Hub
          # Absent on branch dry-runs, which have no context: the snapshot build
          # still exercises the Dockerfile, it just pushes nothing.
          command: |
            if [ -z "${DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME:-}" ]; then
              echo "No Docker Hub credentials — skipping login (snapshot builds do not push)."
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "$DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD" | docker login --username "$DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME" --password-stdin

  store_results:
    steps:
      - store_test_results:
          path: ./test-reports

executors:
  linux:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: large.gen3

  # Arm64 counterpart to `linux`, for checking both halves of a multi-arch
  # image. Deliberately small: it only pulls and runs a container.
  linux-arm:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: arm.medium

  macos:
    macos:
      xcode: 26.5.0

  windows:
    machine: true
    resource_class: windows.medium

jobs:
  check:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:check
      - store_results

  test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:test
      - store_results

  deploy:
    executor: linux
    parameters:
      # Run before anything is installed, so a push with nothing to release
      # stops cheaply.
      gate_steps:
        type: steps
        default: []
      publish_steps:
        type: steps
        default:
          - run: task ci:release
    steps:
      - setup
      - steps: << parameters.gate_steps >>
      - setup-docker
      - run: sudo apt update --yes
      - run:
          name: Install snapcraft
          command: |
            sudo apt install snapd --yes
            sudo snap install snapcraft --classic
      - run:
          name: Install choco
          command: |
            sudo cp tools/choco.sh /usr/local/bin/choco
            sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/choco
            choco help
      - steps: << parameters.publish_steps >>
      - store_artifacts:
          path: dist

  smoke-test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
      install-steps:
        type: steps
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - steps: << parameters.install-steps >>
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci binary
          command: circleci version

  # Matrixed over the executors rather than over the tags: only the architecture
  # needs a machine of its own, so each job checks both variants. Printing the
  # arch inside the container makes the log say which half of the manifest ran. A
  # tag missing this platform fails here anyway — the arm machine images carry no
  # binfmt, so there is nothing to silently emulate an amd64-only image with.
  smoke-test-docker:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1 sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'

  # Opens or updates the release PR (see RELEASE.md).
  release-pr:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:release-pr

  docs:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run:
          name: Generate reference and build the site
          command: task docs:build
      - run:
          name: Check internal links
          command: task docs:test
      - store_artifacts:
          path: docs/website/public
      - persist_to_workspace:
          root: .
          paths:
            - "docs/website/public"

  docs-publish:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - attach_workspace:
          at: .
      - run:
          name: Publish to gh-pages
          command: task ci:docs:publish

  ok-to-deploy:
    type: no-op

workflows:
  ci:
    jobs:
      # gh-pages holds only generated HTML — never run CI on it. Entry jobs (no
      # `requires`) must opt out explicitly; downstream jobs are gated by these.

      - check:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - test:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - macos
                - windows
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - docs:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - deploy:
          name: dry-run
          publish_steps:
            - run: task ci:build
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore:
                - main
                - gh-pages

      - ok-to-deploy:
          requires:
            - check
            - test
            - docs
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - release-pr:
          # One at a time, so two pushes can't race to rewrite release/next.
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/release-pr
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release

      # Publishes only on the push that merges the release PR; halts otherwise.
      - deploy:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/deploy
          gate_steps:
            - run:
                name: Halt unless the release is unpublished
                command: task ci:halt-unless-unreleased
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release
            - macos-codesigning

      - docs-publish:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/docs-publish
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-snap
          executor: linux
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install snapd
                command: sudo apt update --yes && sudo apt install snapd --yes
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Snap stable channel
                # /snap/bin has to be prepended, not just present: the machine
                # image ships its own circleci in /usr/local/bin, which would
                # otherwise shadow the snap and make this job verify the build
                # agent's CLI instead of the release.
                command: |
                  sudo snap install circleci
                  echo 'export PATH="/snap/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-brew
          executor: macos
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Homebrew preview tap
                command: |
                  brew update
                  rm -f /opt/homebrew/bin/circleci
                  brew install circleci-public/circleci/circleci@next
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test-docker:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - linux-arm
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-choco
          executor: windows
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Chocolatey
                command: choco install circleci-cli -y
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

I found some, though the cause isn't a lot of separate jobs. Your `linux` executor is `large.gen3` (4 cores / 16 GiB), and almost every Linux job in the config uses it. Only `test-linux` actually needs that much.

I checked the latest successful run on `main` (`2f7e0fe6…`, merge of PR #2030). Usage is sampled every 15 seconds, and a job counts as oversized when it peaks under about 50% of both CPU and memory.

| Job | Resource class | Peak CPU | Peak memory | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test-linux | large.gen3 | **85%** | 17% | Right size: it needs the cores |
| check | large.gen3 | 51% (about 2 of 4 cores) | 13% | Borderline. 2 cores would be close to full |
| docs | large.gen3 | 29% | 10% | **Oversized** |
| release-pr | large.gen3 | 6% | 6% | **Oversized** |
| smoke-test-snap | large.gen3 | 14% | 6% | **Oversized** |
| smoke-test-docker-linux | large.gen3 | not sampled (about 10s) | – | Very likely oversized: it only runs two `docker run`s, and its arm twin peaks at about 1.2 cores |
| docs-publish | large.gen3 | not sampled (about 8s) | – | Very likely oversized |
| deploy | large.gen3 | not sampled | – | **No data.** It stopped at its release check after 6 seconds. A real release does multi-arch docker builds, so I'd leave it as is |
| smoke-test-docker-linux-arm | arm.medium | 58% | 12% | Fine |
| test-macos | m4pro.medium | 40% | 30% | Under the threshold, but I didn't check whether a cheaper macOS class exists |
| smoke-test-brew | m4pro.medium | 17% | 22% | Same as above |
| test-windows | windows.medium | **100%** | 30% | Maxes out the CPU. If anything it's too small |
| smoke-test-choco | windows.medium | 5% | 15% | Not much to save: that's probably already the smallest Windows class |

**What I'd change:** in `.circleci/config.yml`, add a second Linux executor on a smaller machine class (2 cores / 8 GB). Move `docs`, `docs-publish`, `release-pr`, `smoke-test-snap` and the `linux` entry of `smoke-test-docker` onto it. Keep `linux` (`large.gen3`) for `test-linux` and `deploy`. `check` could move too, but it would use about 100% of 2 cores and likely run a bit slower, so try it and compare run times. The config already does this on the ARM side: `linux-arm` is `arm.medium`, with a comment saying the smoke test only pulls and runs a container.

**How sure this is:**
- It's based on one run. Several jobs lasted 15 seconds or less, so they got one sample or none, and short spikes could be missed. Checking a few more `main` runs before changing anything would make this more reliable.
- The `dry-run` job (the `deploy` job on branches) wasn't in this run, so I have no numbers for it.
- I haven't checked the exact name of the smaller gen3 machine class. Look it up in CircleCI's resource class docs before editing.

I haven't changed anything.
